 1           Plaintiffs Elizabeth Shipley and Shaun Herod (“Plaintiffs”), by and through counsel, bring this
 2   Class Action Complaint against Defendants Meta Platforms, Inc., and Meta Platforms Technologies, LLC
 3   (collectively “Meta”), individually and on behalf of all others similarly situated, and allege, upon personal
 4   knowledge as to their own actions, and upon information and belief as to all other matters, as follows:
 5                                          NATURE OF THE ACTION
 6           1.     Plaintiffs, on behalf of themselves and all other similarly situated Class Members, bring this
 7   putative class action against Meta1 arising from its deceptive bait-and-switch scheme of designing,
 8   manufacturing, distributing, advertising, marketing, and selling its Meta Portal smart device to consumers,

 9   and then unilaterally rendering the devices significantly less functional and largely obsolete.
10           2.     Boasting the Meta Portal as a “step forward in smart video calling” and a new way to “share
11   deeper connections and delightful moments” with friends and families, Meta prominently advertised that
12   the Meta Portal smart device provided numerous features and functions through first-party and third-party
13   applications, such as video-calling, streaming, effects, storytelling, and voice command. Plaintiffs and
14   Class Members purchased the Meta Portal devices believing they would have continued software
15   functionality and based on the myriad of uses that Meta touted.
16           3.     But these promises were short-lived. Only a few years after the Meta Portal first launched,
17   Meta decided to “brick” Meta Portal by stripping many of its software applications and functionality—
18   long before the actual physical device has reached the end of its useful life. As a result of Meta’s unilateral
19   decision to strip Meta Portal of much of its functionality by cutting off many of the features from an
20   otherwise functioning device, Plaintiffs and Class Members are left with devices with significantly less
21   functionality than what they purchased.
22           4.     Plaintiffs and Class Members would not have purchased the Meta Portal devices or would
23   have paid substantially less for them had they known that Meta would abandon all support, remove many
24   software applications, and render the devices less functional despite having many years left in their physical
25   useful life.

 6           26.     The continued software functionality of the costly Meta Portal devices was a substantial
 7   factor in Plaintiffs and Class Members decision to purchase the devices. In other words, Plaintiffs and
 8   Class Members purchased costly Meta Portal devices in reliance upon Defendants’ misrepresentation that

 9   the devices included such features, and its omission that it would cut these features from an otherwise
10   functioning device in just a few years. Had they known that Meta would unilaterally make the device
11   significantly less functional, Plaintiffs and Class Members would not have purchased Meta Portal or would
12   have paid substantially less for it.
13           27.     At the time of purchasing their Meta Portal devices, Plaintiffs and Class Members had no
14   reason to believe that Meta would stop supporting the Meta Portal devices’ software despite the fact that
15   the hardware itself would have continued to function long into the future.
16           28.     Upon information and belief, Meta has not issued refunds to any consumers for the
17   discontinued and less functional Meta Portal devices.
18   II.     Meta’s Unilateral Phasing Out and Discontinuance of the Meta Portal Device Constitutes a
19           Deceptive “Software Tethering” and “Bricking” Practice
20           29.     Manufacturers are incentivized to render devices obsolete so that they can manufacture and
21   sell new ones. Increasingly, by failing to support otherwise functional devices with software functionality
22   included at sale, companies like Defendants unilaterally, and, prematurely, decide that devices are obsolete
23   even though the actual hardware of the device itself has not run its useful life and functions perfectly. Left
24   with a device that is either useless or with less software functionality, consumers are forced to buy updated
25   devices—often from the same manufacturers.
26           30.     In a recent staff report, the Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) acknowledged the harm
27   that results when manufacturers cut back on making software updates to “smart” products like the Meta
28   Portal, eventually turning those products in non-functional “bricks” with limited to no use. As the FTC
30                                                         10

31                                   FIRST AMENDED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
           Case 3:25-cv-03324-WHO             Document 18        Filed 06/23/25       Page 11 of 27



 1   explains, the failure to provide software and the failure to disclose the duration of software support is a
 2   deceptive practice that cause consumer harm that they cannot avoid:
 3          Manufacturers marketing a device as having certain features and then subsequently failing
            to provide software updates needed to maintain those features raises concerns about
 4          consumer harm resulting from deceptive practices. A representation, omission or practice
            is deceptive and violates the FTC Act if it is material and likely to mislead a consumer
 5          acting reasonably under the circumstances. Thus, if a manufacturer makes an express or
            implied representation regarding how long the product will function or be useable, it may
 6          be a deceptive practice if the manufacturer fails to disclose how long it will provide
            necessary software updates.
 7
            Similarly, the failure to provide software updates or the failure to disclose the duration of
 8          software support raises concerns about harm consumers cannot avoid. A practice is unfair
            and violates the FTC Act if it is likely to cause substantial injury that could not be reasonably
 9          avoided by consumers and the injury is not outweighed by any offsetting consumer or
            competitive benefits that the sales practice also produces. Thus, when evaluating a
10          manufacturer’s failure to provide updates or its failure to disclose the duration of software
            support it is appropriate to consider the scope of injury caused by the failure, whether this
11          injury is reasonably avoidable by consumers, and whether there may be any offsetting
            benefits arising from the failure to provide software updates or disclosures about the
12          duration of software support.13
13          31.     Non-profit organization, Truth in Advertising (“TINA”), similarly acknowledged this
14   practice as an increasingly prevalent false advertising practice it calls “software tethering,” “which is when
15   a manufacturer uses software to control how a connected device functions after purchase, if it continues to
16   function at all,” and may range from “taking away features that were advertised at the time of purchase or
17   completely ‘bricking’ a device through software updates[.]”14
18          32.     Consumer Reports also highlighted the concern behind companies’ lack of transparency in
19   disclosing the lifespan of a connected smart device before consumers commit to purchasing:
20          The refusal to disclose how long a consumer can expect their connected appliances to stay
            secure and retain the exciting software-based functions that a consumer may have paid extra
21          for is an example of how efforts to turn everyday devices into internet-connected computers
            have left a regulatory loophole that allows manufacturers to infringe on a consumers’ ability
22          to truly own a product. . . .
23          And consumer should know when this potential loss of features or functions will happen
            before they plunk down their hard-earned cash on a device or appliance. Only when
24          consumers can see how long a manufacturer plans to stand by a connected product can they
            make an informed decision about what they are spending their money on. Absent this
25          information, a consumer could spend thousands on a large appliance, only for the features

 3   have called on the FTC “to create clear guidance to address the issue of software tethering which leads to
 4   several consumer harms, including . . . companies selling connected devices only to render them
 5   nonfunctional later using software.” This practice of “‘bricking’ a connected device purchased by a
 6   consumer in many cases [is an] unfair and deceptive practice[.]”16
 7           34.     The FTC Letter explains “how companies are using software tethers in their devices to
 8   infringe on a consumer’s right to own the products they buy.”17 “This software-server connection tethers

 9   the device to the manufacturer, giving the manufacturer post-purchase control of the software and changing
10   the nature of ownership.”18 As a result, “[c]onsumers increasingly face a death by a thousand cuts as
11   connected products they purchase lose their software support or advertised features that may have
12   prompted the original purchase.”19
13           35.     In fact, the FTC Letter explicitly calls out Defendants and their Meta Portal device as an
14   example of a company that has engaged in this deceptive software tethering and bricking practice: “Other
15   companies kill software support and also the device itself, as Facebook did with its Portal product.”20
16   Additional recent examples of software “bricking” in the consumer marketplace include Spotify’s
17   connected Car Thing device that lasted only 22 months, the iKamand temperature regulating device that
18   was discontinued within the same year, Google’s Dropcam cameras, and Amazon’s Halo health and
19   wellness wearable devices, to name a few.21

 1   III.    Plaintiffs’ Experiences

 3           36.    On or around November 12, 2020, while sitting in her home in San Francisco, Plaintiff
 4   Shipley purchased the Meta Portal device directly from Meta’s website. She paid $154 for the Meta Portal
 5   device. Plaintiff Shipley purchased the Meta Portal device after being exposed to online advertisements
 6   that touted the device as an easy way to connect with isolated, elderly family members during lockdown.
 7           37.    The continued software functionality of the Meta Portal device she purchased was a
 8   substantial factor in her decision to buy the devices. For example, Meta Portal’s voice control feature

 9   factored into her purchase, as she was looking for a device that would enable her to talk to her mother who

 1             73.    Inadequate remedy at law. Legal remedies available to Plaintiffs and Class Members are
 2   inadequate because they are not equally prompt and certain and in other ways as efficient as equitable
 3   relief. Damages are not equally certain as restitution because the standard that governs restitution is
 4   different than the standard that governs damages. Hence, the Court may award restitution even if it
 5   determines that Plaintiff and Class members fail to sufficiently adduce evidence to support an award of
 6   damages. Damages and restitution are not necessarily the same amount. Unlike damages, restitution is not
 7   limited to the amount of money the defendant wrongfully acquired plus the legal rate of interest. Equitable
 8   relief, including restitution, entitles a plaintiff to recover all profits from the wrongdoing, even where the

 9   original funds taken have grown far greater than the legal rate of interest would recognize. Legal claims
10   for damages are not equally certain as restitution because claims under the statutes herein entail few
11   elements. In short, significant differences in proof and certainty establish that any potential legal claim
12   cannot serve as an adequate remedy at law. Due to these differences in proof and certainty, equitable relief
13   is appropriate because Plaintiffs may lack an adequate remedy at law for damages. Even if legal remedies
14   may be available, Plaintiffs seek equitable remedies in the alternative to legal remedies which are as of yet
